idiom_name: def stage(src): for rec in src: yield transform(rec) - plus itertools combinators
implementation_notes: Python's iterator protocol and generator syntax absorb the pattern: a filter is a generator function taking an iterable and yielding transformed values, so a pipeline is nested calls (stage3(stage2(stage1(source())))) with no intermediate list and no Filter or Pipe objects; itertools supplies the standard combinators (islice, filterfalse, chain, groupby, accumulate) and generator expressions cover one-liners. The classic structure is only justified when stages are configured at runtime (a list of callables applied in a loop) or distributed, where a queue becomes the pipe. For CPU-bound stages, move work to processes because the GIL prevents parallel execution of these generators.
pitfalls: A generator is exhausted after one pass; reusing it silently produces an empty pipeline instead of raising, which is a classic source of no-op bugs.
An exception anywhere aborts the whole chain because there is no per-stage error channel unless one is added explicitly (for example a sentinel or a dead-letter generator).
CPU-bound stages stay on one core because the GIL serialises Python threads; use multiprocessing or a native library when parallelism is the goal.

variants.name: asyncio.Queue-connected stage coroutines
variants.idiom_name: per-stage coroutines reading asyncio.Queue(maxsize=..) with sentinel shutdown
variants.implementation_notes: When stages must overlap in time or wait on I/O, each filter becomes a coroutine looping over an asyncio.Queue and pushing into the next queue - the queue is the pipe, maxsize makes put() await and therefore applies backpressure, and a sentinel or task cancellation closes the chain. This is the explicit POSA structure reappearing with queues instead of pipes, at the price of a shutdown protocol and event-loop scheduling overhead. Keep the plain generator form unless stages genuinely run concurrently or await different resources; for CPU-bound work use multiprocessing.Queue, since the GIL still serialises coroutine bodies.
variants.code_sketch:
async def stage(src: asyncio.Queue, dst: asyncio.Queue):
    while (item := await src.get()) is not None:
        await dst.put(transform(item))       # put() awaits when maxsize is reached
    await dst.put(None)                      # propagate EOF downstream

q1, q2 = asyncio.Queue(100), asyncio.Queue(100)
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tg.create_task(stage(q1, q2))
    tg.create_task(sink(q2))
pitfalls: The shutdown sentinel must be forwarded by every stage or downstream tasks block on get() forever; cancelling tasks instead requires cleaning up partially written output.
maxsize=0 means unbounded: the queue silently stops applying backpressure and a slow consumer becomes unbounded memory growth.
A blocking call inside a stage coroutine stalls the event loop and therefore every other stage - run blocking work in a thread or process executor.
